source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: decoder-only transformer, MoE in the FFN block, top-k routing (k=1 or 2), shared/dense attention. All numbers below are structural claims, not measurements on any specific platform.

What actually changes between training and inference:
1. Mechanism (concrete): token routing changes from *load-balanced-by-loss* to *load-balanced-by-luck*. In training you add an auxiliary balance loss (and often capacity factor C>1 with token dropping) so expert utilization is roughly uniform across a large global batch. At inference you serve small, correlated batches; the router is frozen, there is no balance loss, and one decode step may send most of its tokens to a handful of experts. Under expert parallelism this converts a balanced all-to-all into a straggler-bound all-to-all: step latency is set by the busiest expert rank, not the average.
2. Compute vs memory shifts sides. Training is throughput/FLOP-bound and MoE genuinely reduces active FLOPs per token (active params = shared + k experts). Decode inference is memory-bandwidth- and capacity-bound: you must keep *all* experts resident even though only k are read per token, so MoE raises HBM footprint and weight-load traffic per useful FLOP. The arithmetic-intensity win largely evaporates at batch size 1.
3. Token dropping is acceptable in training (capacity factor caps expert queues; dropped tokens just skip the FFN) but is usually unacceptable in serving, so inference either uses C=inf/no-drop or drop-less routing, which reintroduces load imbalance as latency variance rather than as quality loss.
4. Parallelism layout usually differs: training commonly uses expert parallelism fused with data/tensor parallelism inside one job; serving often prefers replicating the whole MoE per instance, or splitting prefill and decode (disaggregated serving, e.g. Dynamo/Mooncake-style) so the all-to-all cost lands only where batches are large enough to amortize it.

Boundary condition (where the above stops holding): if the serving batch is large and diverse enough that per-step token counts per expert approach the training-time distribution — roughly, effective tokens per step >> num_experts * k so each expert gets a statistically stable share — the imbalance term becomes second-order and MoE inference behaves like training. Concretely, at batch size 1 decode the imbalance is maximal; the crossover is workload- and topology-specific and must be measured, not assumed.

Falsifiable predictions:
- P1: expert-utilization entropy at inference is strictly lower than at training for the same model, and decreases as serving batch size decreases.
- P2: p99/p50 inter-token latency ratio grows with expert-parallel degree at fixed batch size.
Evidence to collect: per-expert token counts per step, all-to-all time as a fraction of step time (NCCL/comm profiler), TTFT and TPOT percentiles vs batch size, HBM residency.
Rollback gate: if p99 TPOT regresses beyond the SLO or all-to-all exceeds a preset fraction of step time at target load, fall back to a replicated (no expert-parallel) layout or a dense model of equal serving quality.

source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: FFN-level MoE, top-k routing, frozen router at serving time. Structural claims; no platform-specific numbers invented.

Mechanism (concrete): the *batch that the router sees* changes shape. In training the router optimizes over a large global batch with an auxiliary load-balancing loss and a capacity factor; excess tokens for a hot expert are dropped or rerouted, and that loss term actively pushes utilization toward uniform. At inference the router weights are frozen, no balancing pressure exists, and each decode step carries only batch_size tokens per layer. With expert parallelism this means the all-to-all dispatch/combine per MoE layer is straggler-bound: the step ends when the most-loaded expert rank finishes, so effective throughput tracks the max, not the mean, of the expert load distribution.

Second-order consequences worth naming:
- Cost model inverts. Training cares about active FLOPs per token, where MoE wins. Decode cares about bytes moved per token and total resident weights, where MoE loses: all experts sit in HBM, only k are used.
- Prefill and decode diverge. Prefill has thousands of tokens per step, so expert load is near-uniform and MoE looks like training. Decode has batch_size tokens per step and is the imbalance-sensitive phase. This is a direct argument for prefill/decode disaggregation.
- Token dropping is a training-only tolerance. Serving normally runs drop-less, converting a quality knob into a latency-variance knob.

Boundary condition: the training/inference gap is negligible when tokens per step per MoE layer is large relative to num_experts (rule of thumb: >> num_experts/k tokens per step), because the multinomial routing distribution then concentrates. At small decode batch it is maximal. Also, if the deployment replicates all experts per GPU instead of sharding them (no expert parallelism), there is no all-to-all and the imbalance shows up only as unused FLOPs, not as a collective straggler — at the cost of HBM.

Falsifiable test: hold model and prompts fixed, sweep decode batch size 1 -> 256, and plot (a) expert-load coefficient of variation and (b) fraction of step time in all-to-all. Prediction: both decrease monotonically with batch size.
Evidence required: per-expert token histograms per step, NCCL/comm profile of dispatch+combine, TPOT p50/p99, HBM usage, quality parity check on a held-out eval.
Rollback gate: revert to replicated-expert or dense serving if all-to-all share exceeds the preset budget or p99 TPOT violates SLO at target QPS.

source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: transformer with MoE FFN layers, top-k gating, expert parallelism available but optional. I distinguish structural facts from estimates and give no vendor-specific numbers.

Concrete mechanism that changes: capacity handling. During training you set a capacity factor C (tokens per expert per batch <= C * tokens/num_experts) and you *drop or reroute* overflow tokens; an auxiliary load-balancing loss simultaneously trains the router toward uniform utilization. At inference both of those disappear: the router is frozen and dropping tokens would silently corrupt user output, so serving typically runs drop-less. The overflow that training absorbed as a small quality cost now materializes as a latency cost — the all-to-all dispatch/combine in each MoE layer completes only when the slowest expert rank does.

Other real shifts:
- Bound changes from compute to memory. Training: MoE reduces active FLOPs/token, which is the binding constraint. Decode: the binding constraint is HBM capacity plus weight-read bandwidth, and MoE must keep every expert resident while touching only k. So MoE's efficiency advantage is much larger in training than in single-stream decode.
- Batch statistics change. Prefill (thousands of tokens/step) resembles training; decode (batch_size tokens/step) does not.
- Numerics/kernels differ: training often uses fused grouped-GEMM with a fixed capacity shape; drop-less inference needs variable-length grouped GEMM or padding, which can waste FLOPs or force recompilation on shape changes.

Boundary condition: none of the imbalance story matters if experts are *replicated* rather than sharded — with all experts on every GPU there is no all-to-all, so imbalance costs only idle FLOPs. That layout is feasible only while total expert weights fit in per-GPU HBM alongside the KV cache; once they do not, you are forced into expert parallelism and the straggler effect returns.

Falsifiable hypothesis: for a fixed model, moving from expert-parallel to expert-replicated serving reduces p99 TPOT at batch size 1 but reduces max concurrency (fewer KV-cache slots). Test by measuring both layouts at iso-hardware.
Evidence required: HBM breakdown (weights vs KV vs activations), per-expert token counts, all-to-all time share, TTFT/TPOT percentiles, max concurrent sequences, output-parity check between layouts.
Rollback gate: abandon the expert-parallel layout if it fails the p99 SLO at target concurrency, or if KV-cache capacity forces a preemption rate above the agreed threshold.

source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: MoE placed in FFN blocks, top-k routing, attention dense. Claims are structural; anything numeric below is an explicitly labeled estimate.

Mechanism (concrete): the load-balancing objective is removed at inference. Training adds an auxiliary loss (and often router z-loss) that pushes expert assignment toward uniform over a large global batch, plus a capacity factor that caps per-expert queues. At serving time the router is frozen and there is no balancing pressure; a decode step routes only batch_size tokens per layer. Under expert parallelism the per-layer all-to-all (dispatch then combine) is a synchronizing collective, so step latency = slowest expert rank. Therefore MoE inference latency is governed by the *maximum* of the expert-load distribution while MoE training throughput is governed by its *mean*.

What else genuinely differs:
- Resource bound flips: active-FLOP savings (training's win) vs all-expert HBM residency and weight-read bandwidth (decode's cost).
- Failure mode flips: training absorbs imbalance as dropped tokens (quality); inference absorbs it as tail latency (SLO).
- Phase asymmetry: prefill behaves like training because tokens/step is large; decode does not. This motivates disaggregating prefill and decode onto separate pools with different parallelism, as in Mooncake/Dynamo-style architectures, so the all-to-all runs where it is amortized.

Boundary condition: the divergence collapses when the serving system aggregates enough concurrent requests that tokens per MoE layer per step greatly exceeds num_experts/k. Estimate (not measured): with 64 experts and k=2, you need on the order of hundreds of tokens per step before per-expert counts are statistically stable. Below that, expect high variance; above it, MoE decode approaches its training-time efficiency profile.

Falsifiable predictions:
- P1: expert-load coefficient of variation scales roughly as 1/sqrt(tokens per step).
- P2: disabling expert parallelism (replicating experts) removes the correlation between load imbalance and step latency.
Evidence required: per-step per-expert token histograms, comm profiler traces for dispatch/combine, TPOT p50/p95/p99 vs concurrency, HBM residency, iso-quality eval to confirm no accuracy drift between layouts.
Rollback gate: if measured all-to-all share exceeds the preset budget or p99 TPOT breaches SLO at target load, roll back to expert-replicated serving or to a quality-matched dense model.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Misleading intuition: "A Mixture-of-Experts model with N total parameters but only k active experts costs about the same to serve as a dense model with that active parameter count." People read '8x7B, ~13B active' as '13B to deploy'.

Why it is wrong (concrete mechanism): active parameters determine *FLOPs per token*, not *bytes resident* and not *bytes moved*. Every expert must sit in HBM because the router may select any of them at any token, so memory capacity scales with total parameters, not active ones. Worse, in autoregressive decode the kernel is weight-bandwidth-bound: at small batch you pay to read a fresh set of expert weights per token, and different tokens in the same batch may select different experts, so the batch cannot amortize a single weight read the way a dense FFN can. Add the per-MoE-layer all-to-all (dispatch + combine) under expert parallelism, which is a synchronizing collective whose cost tracks the *most loaded* expert rank, and the deployment cost of the MoE is much closer to its total-parameter footprint than to its active-parameter FLOP count.

Corrected statement: MoE buys you dense-model-quality at reduced *compute* per token; it does not buy you reduced *memory* or reduced *serving complexity*. Budget HBM against total expert weights plus KV cache; budget latency against all-to-all and expert-load imbalance.

Boundary condition (when the naive intuition is nearly right): in large-batch prefill or offline batch scoring, where thousands of tokens per step are routed, per-expert weight reads are amortized across many tokens and the workload becomes compute-bound. There the MoE really does behave close to its active-parameter cost. The intuition fails hardest at batch size 1 decode.

Falsifiable prediction: measure tokens/s/GPU for the MoE and for a dense model with the same active parameter count. Prediction: near parity at large-batch prefill, and a significant MoE deficit at batch-size-1 decode; the MoE will also support fewer concurrent sequences at equal HBM because expert weights crowd out KV cache.
Evidence required: HBM breakdown (weights/KV/activations), tokens-per-step per-expert histograms, all-to-all fraction of step time, TTFT/TPOT percentiles at matched concurrency, max concurrency at fixed SLO.
Rollback gate: if MoE cannot meet the p99 TPOT SLO at the concurrency needed for the cost target, revert to the quality-matched dense baseline.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Misleading intuition: "MoE routing is basically free — it is just a small linear layer picking top-k experts, so the overhead is negligible."

Why it is wrong (concrete mechanism): the router matmul is indeed tiny, but the router's *output* triggers a data movement pattern, and that is the real cost. After gating you must permute tokens so each expert receives a contiguous block, exchange them across ranks with an all-to-all (dispatch), run grouped GEMMs of ragged sizes, then all-to-all again (combine) and un-permute. Under expert parallelism this is two synchronizing collectives per MoE layer per step. Because it is synchronizing, its cost is set by the most-loaded expert rank, not the average — so a frozen router that happens to favor a few experts on a small decode batch inflates every step. The permute/un-permute and ragged grouped-GEMM also cost real memory traffic and can force padding or shape-driven kernel recompiles.

Corrected statement: routing compute is negligible; routing-induced communication, memory permutation, and load imbalance are not. Model MoE overhead as 2 all-to-alls per MoE layer plus a load-imbalance multiplier, not as one small GEMM.

Boundary condition (when the intuition is approximately true): if experts are replicated on every GPU rather than sharded, there is no all-to-all at all — routing collapses to a local mask and its overhead really is small. This layout is only viable while total expert weights plus KV cache fit in per-GPU HBM. Likewise, in a single-node deployment with high-bandwidth intra-node interconnect and large batches, the all-to-all can be small relative to compute.

Falsifiable prediction: profile the same model with expert parallelism on and off at fixed batch size. Prediction: with EP on, all-to-all plus permute occupies a measurable, non-trivial share of MoE-layer time and that share grows as batch size shrinks and as EP degree grows; with EP off the share is ~0 but HBM headroom and max concurrency drop.
Evidence required: NCCL/comm profile split into dispatch vs combine, kernel-level timeline showing permute/un-permute, per-expert token counts, TPOT percentiles vs EP degree and batch size, HBM breakdown.
Rollback gate: if the measured collective share exceeds the pre-agreed budget of step time at target load, roll back to expert replication or reduce EP degree.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Misleading intuition: "Adding more experts adds capacity for free, because active compute per token stays fixed at top-k." The implied conclusion is that scaling experts is a costless quality lever.

Why it is wrong (concrete mechanism): holding k fixed does hold FLOPs per token roughly fixed, but three costs scale with the *number* of experts. (1) Memory: all experts must be resident, so HBM for weights grows linearly with expert count and directly crowds out KV cache, reducing max concurrency at fixed hardware. (2) Communication: under expert parallelism, more experts usually means a larger expert-parallel group, and the all-to-all's message-count/latency term grows with group size, while each message shrinks — pushing the collective toward the latency-bound regime where interconnect round-trips, not bandwidth, dominate. (3) Statistics: with more experts and a fixed number of tokens per step, expected tokens per expert falls, so relative load imbalance rises (variance of a multinomial split grows in relative terms as bins increase). Since the all-to-all is synchronizing, tail load sets step latency.

Corrected statement: more experts trades *memory and communication* for *quality at fixed active FLOPs*. It is a real lever but its price is paid in HBM footprint, collective latency, and tail-latency variance — none of which appear in an active-parameter count.

Boundary condition (when it is closest to free): during large-batch prefill or offline scoring, where tokens per step greatly exceeds num_experts/k, per-expert load concentrates and the collective is bandwidth-bound and well amortized. Then added experts cost mainly HBM. The intuition fails hardest at small-batch decode with a high expert count.

Falsifiable prediction: sweep expert count (or EP degree) at fixed active parameters and fixed batch size. Prediction: HBM for weights grows ~linearly, max concurrency falls, expert-load coefficient of variation rises, and p99 TPOT degrades faster than p50.
Evidence required: HBM breakdown, per-expert token histograms, all-to-all latency vs message size and group size, TTFT/TPOT percentiles, max concurrency at fixed SLO, held-out quality delta to confirm the capacity actually bought accuracy.
Rollback gate: reject the larger-expert-count configuration if quality gain is inside eval noise, or if p99 TPOT or max concurrency breaches the SLO/cost target.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Misleading intuition: "Each expert specializes in a human-interpretable domain — one does code, one does math, one does biology — so you can shard or prune experts by topic."

Why it is wrong (concrete mechanism): routing is learned jointly with the balance loss, at *token* granularity, per *layer*. The auxiliary load-balancing loss explicitly pushes assignments toward uniform utilization, which actively discourages the kind of coarse topical clustering people imagine; empirically reported specialization is usually at the level of token identity, position, or syntactic role, and it differs layer by layer. A single request's tokens therefore scatter across many experts at every MoE layer, and the set changes between layers. Consequences: you cannot route a whole request to a topic-specific subset, you cannot safely prune 'irrelevant' experts for a domain deployment without measuring quality loss, and you cannot assume topic-based expert placement will reduce cross-rank traffic.

Corrected statement: treat expert assignment as a learned, token-level, layer-local load-balanced partition, not a semantic taxonomy. Any capacity or placement decision based on experts must be justified by measured routing statistics on *your* traffic, not by an interpretability story.

Boundary condition (when something like the intuition holds): if the model was trained with explicit domain- or language-conditioned routing, or with routing at sequence/task granularity rather than token granularity, then request-level expert affinity can be real and exploitable. Similarly, strongly skewed production traffic can produce a stable, measurable hot-expert set — but that is an empirical property of your workload, not a general property of MoE.

Falsifiable prediction: log per-layer expert assignments for a domain-homogeneous request set (e.g. all Python code). Prediction: the assignment distribution will be much closer to uniform than a topic-specialization story implies, and the top-experts set will differ substantially across layers and across two different domains' request sets.
Evidence required: per-layer per-expert token counts by domain, mutual information between input domain label and expert choice, and — before any pruning — held-out quality with and without the pruned experts.
Rollback gate: do not ship any expert pruning or affinity-based routing unless measured quality on the target domain is within the agreed tolerance and the routing-affinity signal is reproducible across traffic samples; otherwise revert to the full expert set.

source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.

Misleading intuition: "MoE load balancing is solved — the auxiliary balance loss during training guarantees experts stay evenly used in production."

Why it is wrong (concrete mechanism): the balance loss is a *training-time* gradient signal computed over a large, diverse global batch. It shapes the router weights so that assignments are uniform *in expectation over that distribution*. At serving time the router is frozen, the loss no longer exists, and each decode step routes only batch_size tokens per layer — a tiny sample. Even a perfectly calibrated router yields high relative variance when tokens per step is small compared to num_experts/k. Worse, production traffic is not i.i.d. with the training mixture: a burst of same-language or same-format requests correlates token distributions and reliably creates hot experts. Because the expert-parallel all-to-all is a synchronizing collective, the slowest rank sets the step time, so imbalance shows up as tail latency (p99 TPOT), not as an averaged-away inefficiency.

Corrected statement: training-time balancing makes the *expected* distribution uniform; it does nothing about small-sample variance or distribution shift at serving. Balance must be monitored and mitigated at runtime — via larger effective batches, expert replication for hot experts, capacity-aware scheduling, or dropping expert parallelism entirely.

Boundary condition (when the intuition is nearly right): large-batch prefill or offline batch inference over a diverse corpus, where tokens per step >> num_experts/k and traffic resembles the training mixture. There, measured utilization really can be close to uniform and the residual imbalance is second-order.

Falsifiable prediction: instrument production routing. Prediction: expert-load coefficient of variation is materially higher in decode than in prefill on the same model, and higher during correlated traffic bursts than during mixed traffic; p99/p50 TPOT ratio will track that CV.
Evidence required: per-step per-expert token histograms segmented by prefill vs decode and by traffic segment, all-to-all wait time per rank, TPOT percentiles, and a controlled replay of a bursty traffic window.
Rollback gate: if measured CV or p99 TPOT exceeds the agreed threshold under replayed peak traffic, roll back to expert-replicated serving (accepting lower max concurrency) or reduce expert-parallel degree before shipping.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for MoE. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer:
Goal: decide, with a falsifiable test, whether an MoE checkpoint beats a quality-matched dense baseline for a specific serving workload. Everything below is a design; no results are claimed.

Hypothesis (H1): at iso-quality on a held-out eval and iso-hardware, the MoE delivers higher tokens/s/GPU at the target p99 TPOT SLO.
Null (H0): the MoE meets neither the throughput gain threshold nor the SLO, or its gain vanishes once concurrency is matched.

Controls to hold fixed (state these or the experiment is meaningless): hardware and interconnect topology, dtype/quantization, tokenizer, max context, scheduler and batching policy (continuous batching), KV-cache layout and eviction, sampling parameters, request trace (replayed, identical seed and arrival times), and server version. Baseline selection rule: pick the dense model by *matched held-out quality*, not matched parameter count — otherwise you are measuring a quality/throughput trade and calling it an MoE win.

Concrete mechanism under test: MoE cuts active FLOPs per token (active = shared + top-k experts) but adds (a) router + permute/un-permute, (b) two all-to-alls per MoE layer under expert parallelism, whose cost tracks the most-loaded rank, and (c) full-expert HBM residency, which crowds out KV cache and therefore caps concurrency.

Procedure:
1. Quality gate first. Run the held-out eval; if the MoE is not within the agreed quality band of the dense baseline, stop — no throughput number is meaningful.
2. Sweep offered load from 10% to 120% of expected peak on the replayed trace, with two length mixes (e.g. 2k in / 256 out and 8k in / 1k out).
3. For each point record: TTFT and TPOT p50/p95/p99, tokens/s/GPU, max concurrent sequences, queue/preemption rate, HBM breakdown (weights / KV / activations), per-expert token histograms, and the all-to-all share of MoE-layer time.
4. Ablation: rerun the MoE with expert parallelism off (experts replicated). This isolates collective cost from raw MoE compute.
5. Repeat each point at least 3 times; report medians and dispersion. Discard the first run as warm-up (compile/graph capture, cache fill).

Boundary condition: the comparison is only valid inside the concurrency range where both systems meet the p99 SLO. If the MoE wins on tokens/s/GPU only at a concurrency it cannot actually sustain within SLO, or only after its HBM footprint has cut max concurrency below the production requirement, the win is not real. Also, results at batch size 1 do not generalize to large-batch prefill and vice versa — report both phases separately.

Decision / rollback gate: adopt the MoE only if (i) quality is within band, (ii) tokens/s/GPU improves by more than the measured run-to-run dispersion at the target SLO, and (iii) max concurrency meets the production requirement. Otherwise keep the dense baseline. Pre-register these thresholds before running.
